Photograph: South Yorkshire Police/PA UK news Man killed by tiger at Yorkshire zoo had bouts of psychosis, inquest hears William Chapman’s family describe ‘severe distress’ after Donald Trump shares footage of the attack on social media Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man who was killed by a tiger at a South Yorkshire zoo had suffered bouts of psychosis, his family told an inquest opening, as they expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services before his death. William Chapman was mauled to death by the animal at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster on Saturday, after climbing into its enclosure. The 24-year-old had been diagnosed with schizophrenia but was “highly functioning and independent with no care requirements”, the hearing at Doncaster coroner’s court heard. He was under the care of local mental health services, however, the coroner’s officer Caitlin Brookes said his family had expressed “a number of concerns” in relation to his contact with them. Brookes said the Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS foundation trust had launched an investigation following Chapman’s death. The inquest heard Chapman was a self-employed online trader who was living in Doncaster at the time of his death. An initial postmortem examination found that he had died from multiple traumatic injuries after his encounter with the tiger. The inquest heard he attended Yorkshire Wildlife Park on 10 October, and at about 1.30pm, climbed over two fences and entered the enclosure housing the 200kg male Siberian tiger named Altai. Brookes said: “He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining multiple traumatic injuries which rapidly led to his death.” Park staff secured the tiger, and paramedics attended but confirmed Chapman’s death at the scene. The senior coroner, Nicola Mundy, said her office was awaiting a more substantial report as to the extent of Chapman’s injuries. The inquest heard Chapman’s stepfather had travelled to the mortuary to identify him on 13 October. The inquest heard his full name was William Harry Bruce Chapman and that he was born in 2002 in Chichester. Mundy said Chapman’s family “were finding things incredibly difficult” and had decided not to attend the hearing, but would be updated afterwards by her staff. View image in fullscreen Flowers left at the entrance of Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster, in tribute to Chapman. Photograph: Dave Higgens/PA His family spoke out on Wednesday after the US president, Donald Trump, shared a video of the attack on Tuesday to his 13 million followers on Truth Social. He followed this with an AI-generated video of himself play fighting with the tiger, which ends with him and the tiger hugging. Chapman’s family said online footage being shared was “deeply offensive” and causing them “severe distress”. They also shared a tribute to him, writing: “William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back. Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication.” As a child, Chapman appeared in ITV’s 2009 comedy drama May Contain Nuts and in BBC Learning’s True Stories series, according to IMDb. He previously attended Jackie Palmer stage school in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, which paid tribute on Facebook and posted a picture of Chapman as a child student. City of Doncaster Council, which is responsible for licensing the park, is carrying out a health and safety investigation and said it would share the outcome with the coroner, the hearing was told. Wildlife and zoo experts previously told the Guardian it was unlikely Yorkshire Wildlife Park could have done anything to prevent the death. The park said staff were receiving specialist support and that Altai, a member of an endangered species, would not be euthanised. A full inquest will be held on 18 March next year. Photograph: Smirnov Vladimir/Anadolu/Getty Opinion Infectious diseases The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information Editorial In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics Sun 18 Oct 2026 17.30 BST Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 17.39 BST Share I s there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases. It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future. The key to containing an outbreak is quick disclosure and open sharing of information. Russia reportedly held high-level meetings about the case, quarantined the hospital where the worker was treated and traced about 200 contacts. That response suggests officials believed the infection was plague, and yet they did not report any of this to the WHO, as international law requires. Russia later revealed that the worker died of a pneumonia of unknown origin – hardly useful information. It undoubtedly gathered lab results and genetic sequences that could shed more light on the case, but has not shared them. View image in fullscreen The logo of the World Health Organization. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Earlier this year, the hantavirus outbreak originating on the MV Hondius cruise ship was successfully contained , showing that the global health system can still work well when countries cooperate. This latest incident suggests that one recalcitrant nation can jeopardise everyone’s safety. It is not the WHO’s fault that Russia is essentially a rogue state, but the body must be ready for such eventualities. International politics is fragmented, and only becoming more so. Earlier this year the US left the WHO (though it is still party to some of its treaties). States follow international laws when they believe in them, or when they believe that there will be penalties – reputational or otherwise – for not playing along. The WHO has not attempted to play hardball with Russia, or set off a round of international condemnation from leading member states. Some might be heartened that on 7 October the US state department officially requested that the Russian government share information with the WHO. However, it is likely that this reflects Washington’s increasingly ad hoc approach to international politics – using every lever available as situations arise – rather than a renewed commitment to international law. President Trump said on the same day that he would speak to Vladimir Putin about the issue. If that happened, no one has heard about it or what information may have been revealed. The keen US interest may give credence to speculation that what in fact happened was some kind of bioweapons research leak. This is thought to be unlikely, but not impossible. The fact that such a scenario can even be plausibly entertained three weeks after the initial event speaks to a serious breakdown in the system. Western states probably do not hold much sway with Russia . But the other Brics nations may have more. The WHO used to rely on US backing for its requests. It may now have to find support among wider, more multipolar coalitions. This potential outbreak may come to nothing, but there will be another soon.
